paper_title: Position: AI Agents in Scientific Teams Should Be Studied as Human-Agent Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model-based agents are increasingly deployed as collaborators in scientific discovery yet most current work focuses on the autonomous capabilities of "AI Scientists". We argue that this overlooks the social aspects of scientific teamwork, and that studying AI Scientists as human-agent systems (HAS)--where the unit of analysis is the human-agent pair--is both underexplored and undervalued. We establish these points through literature and empirical analysis, and highlight recent incidences and studies which show that deploying agents in science without accounting for human-agent dynamics introduces near-term risks, including reduced diversity of scientific inquiry. Through analysis of real-world case studies, we show that scientists and agents can augment each other's capabilities. We call for new research that adopts the HAS lens to develop mathematical frameworks for understanding and fostering human-AI synergy in scientific discovery.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern science is social endeavor that increasingly involves working in teams (Fortunato et al., 2018; NASEM, 2025). Collaboration helps scientists achieve their lofty goals by bringing experts with diverse scientific backgrounds and experiences together, combining their strengths to collectively answer highly complex questions. Science teams vary widely in their form and function, from small university laboratories to large institutions that coordinate hundreds of members. Meta-analysis of scientific teamwork has found that working in team increases impact; in fact, teams are 6.3 times more likely to produce highly cited paper than solo author (Wuchty et al., 2007). Today, scientific teamwork is undergoing major shift as large language model (LLM)-based agentssystems that perceive, reason, and act in an environment, which we refer to simply as agentsare being deployed not only as tools for scientists, but as collaborators in scientific processes. The introduction of agents into scientific teamwork sits within broader trends of 1) increasing prevalence and advantage of scientific teamwork (Hall et al., 2018) and 2) increasing levels of automation in science. Position papers envision AI Scientists as evolving towards higher levels of autonomy with less and less reliance on human judgment and oversight (Gao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b;a; Wei et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025; Tie et al., 2026). In Section 2, we analyze current agentic systems adapted for scientific discovery, which we call AI Scientists, finding that the majority of recent work only considers narrow form of patrick.emami@nlr.gov yasanka.horawalavithana@pnnl.gov 1 Table 1: representative set of agents categorized by the primary channel for human feedback (row-color). See Section 2 for definitions. Fewer systems support interaction geared at sustained, iterative, and joint collaboration typical of human-human teamwork. This literature has largely been isolated from the socio-technical realities of science. If AI Scientists are to be effectively integrated into scientific teams, it is timely that we also begin to study them as human-agent systems (HAS). An HAS considers as core components: agents, human participants, an interface that facilitates human-agent interaction through actions, and the environment which the HAS is situated in (Haupt & Brynjolfsson, 2025; Zou et al., 2025a; Luo et al., 2026). In HAS, the unit of study is the pair: humans and agents. Our position is that studying AI Scientists as HAS is underexplored and undervalued, and that new research which adopts the lens of HAS is needed to develop an understanding of human-AI synergy in scientific discovery settings. We argue that adopting an HAS lens can help us better understandand thus potentially mitigatenear-term risks of deploying AI Scientists at scale. Evidence of the risks of AI in science is accruing; for example, recent study showed that AI-augmented research produces three times as many papers at 5% reduction in the diversity of explored topics (Hao et al., 2026). In Section 3, we provide further evidence from recent incidents and studies, and discuss the importance of framing AI Scientists as HAS to mitigation efforts. We also argue that an HAS perspective presents path to exploring new scientific questions and discovering new solutions inaccessible to humans alone and AI alone. In Section 4, we analyze recent real-world case studies of scientists co-working alongside agents that qualitatively illustrate how humans and agents have augmented each others outputs, achieving level of human-AI synergy that tangibly improved scientific outcomes. Finally, we raise new questions about the study of agents in scientific discovery motivated by the HAS lens in Section 5, and discuss alternative views in Section 6. 2 Table 2: preliminary evaluation of feedback-seeking behavior in ReAct GPT-5-mini agent on the End-to-End Discovery (E2E) AstaBench benchmark. We compare three conditions: (1) the AstaBench planning-centric ReAct agent harness, (2) adding an ask user tool and the HAS human feedback taxonomy to the system prompt as feedback encouragement, and (3) adding explicit guidance to always call the ask user tool before every action. Condition (3) acts as an upper bound on agent disengagements. We use LLM-as-a-judge to classify questions under the taxonomy and show dimension-wise percentages (counts across 10 E2E development set tasks normalized by total questions asked), averaged across three judges for robustness. Key findings: The agent without explicit per-step instruction does not know when to ask, e.g., it prefers to make assumptions about how to handle ambiguous situations when critical resources are unavailable. With per-step enforcement, the dominant feedback type is evaluative, generally occurring mid-task. Second most common behavior is guidance-based, e.g., asking the user their preference given options, occurring heavily in the pre-task phase. Corrective feedback is rarely requested. sections.title: 2 AI Scientists as HAS: A Review and Preliminary Experiment
sections.content: We adopt an HAS lens to review the literature on AI Scientists, with the goal of broadly understanding how current systems interact with human scientists. Our review categorizes AI Scientist systems based on the primary channel which human feedback enters the scientific discovery loop: artifact-level feedback (Section 2.1), discovery phase-level feedback (Section 2.2), research planning feedback (Section 2.3), and asynchronous steering & interruption (Section 2.4). We adopt three human feedback dimensions from Zou et al. (2025a)s taxonomy for LLM HAS in Table 1 to further organize systems: TypeEvaluative (E): assessment of output quality, Guidance (G): instructions, demonstrations, or critiques, or Corrective (C): user edits or fixes, GranularityCoarse (C): Single assessment for an entire output or outcome, Fine (F): Targeted step-wise feedback, and PhaseInitial setup & goal (I): Pre-task, During task execution (D): Mid-task, Post-task eval & refinement (P). 2.1 Artifact-level feedback Early AI Scientist systems automate the full discovery pipelineideation, experimentation, manuscript preparationrequiring humans only to specify research question and evaluate final outputs (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2025b; Tang et al., 2026; Weng et al., 2025b). Tree-search and Bayesian-optimization extensions improve exploration and reduce hallucinations by filtering hypotheses with computational validation (Yamada et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2024b; Yu et al., 2025). Tighter internal feedback loops feed experiment results back into ideation (Yuan et al., 2025) or pair the agent with peer-review trained reviewer model for iterative refinement (Weng et al., 2025a), reducing reliance on human review before final evaluation. Multi-agent variants organize LLM agents into collaborative teams (Su et al., 2025), structured multi-stage workflows (Tang et al., 2026), and swarm reasoning over knowledge graphs (Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2025a); agent preprint servers enable sharing results for cross-lab iteration (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025). Autoresearch demonstrates that simple coding harness and LLM can serve similar role when also equipped with domain-specific tools and an iterative evaluation loop (Karpathy, 2025). In all cases, humans remain as initiator and final evaluator. 2.2 Discovery-phase-level feedback large class of AI Scientists permit humans to intervene after one or more phases of sequential discovery workflow, canonically: literature review, ideation and hypothesis generation, experimentation, then manuscript preparation and review. Across these systems, human feedback is primarily evaluative and corrective; granularity level varies from coarse (fixed review gates) to fine (editable phase-level memory). Multi-agent systems assign phase-specific roles to agents and expose phase-level review gates where scientists provide high-level feedback (Schmidgall et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2025; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Villaescusa-Navarro et al., 2025). Denarios Markdown-based memory system exposes each phase-specific modules inputs and outputs, enabling finegrained oversight by editing intermediate state before resuming execution (VillaescusaNavarro et al., 2025). Transparency and rewind mechanisms (e.g., linking generated figures to source code, reverting to earlier phases) further increase steerability (Ifargan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Phase-specific feedback targets common failure modes such as hypothesis vagueness. Strategies range from high-level textual feedback on ideas (Team et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2024), to fine-grained feedback on complex outputs like 3D crystal structures(Qi et al., 2024), to idea down-selection from ranked pools (Yamada et al., 2025; Jansen et al., 2025). Googles Co-Scientist for hypothesis generation adds generate-debate-evolve tournament over hypotheses, with scientists supplying objectives upfront and steering between roundsyielding experimentally validated discoveries in drug repurposing and antimicrobial resistance (Gottweis et al., 2025). 2.3 Research-plan-level feedback Many scientific activities do not fit the sequential workflows of artifact-level and phaselevel systems, which offer limited visibility into low-level agent actions and restrict human involvement to fixed feedback gates. Planning-centric AI Scientists address this via plancritique-execute paradigm, generating high-level plans and incorporating human feedback before execution (He et al., 2026). Domain-specific systems constrain the planning action space to narrow set of tools and workflows (Zou et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025; Darvish et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025b), with feedback granularity ranging from pre-execution plan critique (Darvish et al., 2025) to per-step approval (Zhou et al., 2025b). The human role here is primarily guidance oriented: scientists proactively shape the agents course of action through collaborative planning rather than reacting to outputs. 2.4 Feedback via asynchronous steering & interruption minority of AI Scientists offer fine-grained, asynchronous human interaction during phased discovery workflows. FreePhDLabor (Li et al., 2025) supports real-time interruption by writing corrective feedback into persistent agent memory. ScienceClaw (Wang et al., 2026) enables scientists to inspect and redirect agents by commenting on the Infinite platform. EvoScientist (Lyu et al., 2026) adopts human-on-the-loop paradigm with self-evolving memory that learns user preferences across sessions. OmniScientist (Shao et al., 2025a) aims at seamless human participation across pipeline phases through collaborative research protocol, peer-review and the human-voted ScienceArena platform. Coding harnesses also support mid-run interruption, but only with continuous monitoring or agents that know when to ask for help  (Table 2)  an open challenge even for frontier LLMs (Gulati et al., 2026). Asynchronous steering and interruption offers the highest level of human control by enabling intervention at arbitrary points rather than only at phase or output boundaries. 2.5 Preliminary empirical support Our synthesis of the literature reveals that most AI Scientists assign humans supervisory rolesscoping, auditing, approvaltreating discovery as an isolated optimization problem weakly tied to human-led research practices. Artifact-level feedback is the most numerous; discovery-phase-level systems that gate input at workflow boundaries form the next tier. Planning-centric systems constitute smaller but growing class, and only handful support flexible asynchronous interaction. To strengthen these findings, we also conduct preliminary experiment on representative planning-based AI Scientist, the ReAct-based agent harness and GPT-5-mini from 4 the AstaBench AI Scientist benchmark suite (Bragg et al., 2025)). We compare variants provided with an ask user tool (Gulati et al., 2026) and increasing levels of feedback guidance. Questions are responded with an automatic continuation prompt (the AstaBench default). The results on 10 End-to-End Discovery tasks in Table 2 suggest there is room for improving the ability of agents to understand when to ask for feedback and how to ask for fine-grained, corrective help in challenging, end-to-end discovery settings. We expand later on the potential benefits of humans and AI Scientists mutually correcting each others mistakes in Section 4. While 10 tasks may appear nominally small, each task represents full, computationally intensive idea-to-report discovery workflow, providing deep rather than broad measure of agent behavior.

sections.title: 3 Studying AI Scientists as HAS can assist near-term risk mitigation
sections.content: Deploying AI Scientists in scientific teams raises pressing epistemic, existential, and ethical questions. We argue that HAS lens helps center human participation in discovery loops, aiding near-term risk mitigation. While future AI Scientists may transcend current limitations, our emphasis is on near-term risks exacerbated when humans offload deliberative processes to AI rather than participating as teammates. 3.1 Can AI Scientists reliably produce accurate and unbiased scientific knowledge? LLMs notoriously hallucinate (Xie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025): post-hoc review found 51 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers containing 100 confirmed hallucinated citations1; ACL 2026 similarly flagged over 100 accepted papers citing non-existent literature2. More broadly, LLMs and agents are prone to fabricating data or results when faced with demanding tasks (Miyai et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025) (also observed in our E2E experiment in Table 2). related concern is bias proliferation: LLMs may over-represent certain paradigms while under-representing novel ideas (Liu et al., 2025). GPT-4-generated college admissions essays were collectively less novel than human-written ones (Moon et al., 2025), with worrisome implications for homogenization of scientific inquiry (Messeri & Crockett, 2024; Hao et al., 2026). An HAS lens calls for systems that maintain human oversight in the near term to detect hallucinations and biases. End-of-process review (Section 2.1) is inadequate; asynchronous interaction at multiple granularitiesincluding audits of trace logs and codecan surface issues earlier (Luo et al., 2025), if accounting for cognitive load introduced by the speed and scale of AI. 3.2 How will AI Scientists affect our scientific institutions and human expertise? AI Scientists output volume strains peer review, which is already overloaded: NeurIPS and ICLR submissions increased 10.4 from 2014 to 2024 without commensurate reviewer growth (Wei et al., 2025b; Xie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). They also expand the attack surface of scientific software and data. Backdoor attacks can induce LLMs to produce malicious code, and poisoning crowd-sourced knowledge bases like Wikipedia can enable such attacks (Souly et al., 2025; Carlini et al., 2024). Perhaps most consequentially, overreliance may cause de-skilling in scientists, especially among junior researchers (Xie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). recent study shows dependence on AI coding assistants reduces conceptual understanding (Shen & Tamkin, 2026). Younger users show higher susceptibility to cognitive offloading (Gerlich, 2025). The HAS lens pushes us to maintain institutional health as we deploy AI Scientists. Automated governancered teaming (Ge et al., 2024), adversarial evaluations, monitoring, and provenance trackingcan address misuse and security. The de-skilling question points more directly to HAS design: how we interact with AI systems matters for skill formation (Shen 1https://gptzero.me/news/neurips/ 2https://2026.aclweb.org/acl statement/ 5 & Tamkin, 2026), making HAS research an important lever for preserving the deliberate practice through which scientists develop competencies. 3.3 Who is responsible when AI Scientists cause harm or enable misuse? When AI Scientists facilitate research in harmful or sensitive areas, accountability is unclear. NIST recognizes AI as uniquely exacerbating risks of enhancing chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons capabilities (AI, 2024). Legal liability for AI harms remains rapidly evolving. LLM-based systems also heighten concerns about unintentional plagiarism: even when text is not verbatim, determining originality is difficult. An expert review found 36% of LLM and AI Scientist-generated papers contained noticeable plagiarism (Gupta & Pruthi, 2025). Research on whether human involvement at consequential decision points preserves accountability (Rahwan et al., 2019) would benefit both scientific quality and safety. Designing human-agent interfaces with natural intervention opportunities and plagiarism detection tools that do not overburden peer review are important topics for future study.

sections.title: 4 The potential of human-AI synergy in science: case studies
sections.content: We now turn to human-AI synergy, general goal of any HAS. In HAS, information and capability asymmetries are key driver of effective collaboration (Hemmer et al., 2025), creating opportunities for humans and AI to complement each other and outperform either member alone. Prior work has formalized synergy as complementary team performance in classification decision support, combining human and AI predictions to reduce errors (Bansal et al., 2021; Steyvers et al., 2022). Empirically, complementarity appears rarely (Vaccaro et al., 2024), though this may reflect structural barriers: incentives favor autonomy research over HAS, and costly human studies limit rigorous evaluation (Haupt & Brynjolfsson, 2025). weaker but still important form is human augmentation, where AI assists people without requiring proof that AI cannot do better alone. Both complementarity and augmentation have the potential to greatly benefit scientific discovery. Each case study explored next is drawn from published account of working scientist collaborating with an agent on concrete scientific task. Together they illustrate patterns of mutual augmentation: humans contributing conceptual framing, domain judgment, and epistemic verification; agents compressing implementation while also contributing at the conceptual level. 4.1 Case study #1: Vibe-coding minor complexity-theory result with Gemini 3 Pro This case study, obtained from the collection by Woodruff et al. (2026), concerns complexity theorist collaborating with Gemini 3 Pro inside Google Antigravity (a LATEX-integrated IDE) to write up theorem they had not previously had time to publish. How AI augmented humans: Given an initial prompt to plan and draft the paper in the human authors writing style, Gemini generated structured roadmap (plan.md) and draft manuscript (paper.tex), then iteratively expanded proofs and exposition over eight prompt turns. This reduced the overhead of assembling the proof details on paper plus drafting and organizing publishable write-up of result that might otherwise have remained informal. How humans augmented AI: Human expertise was decisive at key steering points. Early in the process, the human expert identified missing technical context (including relevant prior work and search-vs.-decision framing) and corrected an erroneous assumption in lemma. The interaction succeeded because an expert could diagnose omissions and provide high-quality feedback; without that expertise, the same workflow would likely fail or produce misleading paper. The synergy: The workflow resembles an expert-plus-junior-collaborator pattern, where the human sets the research direction and quality standards while the agent accelerates drafting and execution. The case illustrates synergy that enabled minor-result publication, but it also surfaces risk raised in Section 3: if widely adopted, this interaction mode may 6 homogenize scientific writing and may be especially risky for early-career scientists who still need to develop core writing and reasoning skills through deliberate practice. 4.2 Case study #2: AI-assisted reduced physics modeling of thermonuclear burn propagation with GPT-5 This case study, from Bubeck et al. (2025), concerns an expert collaborating with GPT-5 through the ChatGPT interface to develop reduced physics model of thermonuclear burn initiation and propagation. The exercise spanned four linked activities: (1) setting up simplified PDE-based model for physical intuition, (2) implementing numerical simulation, (3) designing numerical experiments to expose key sensitivities, and (4) developing theory to explain the simulation outcomes. The expert reported that the strongest outcome of this exercise was not time saving; rather it was (4) theory-level explanation tying known physical relations into closed-form predictor, used to verify that the numerically elicited trends were physically coherent. How AI augmented humans: GPT-5 helped translate human-provided concept into concrete computational workflow. It drafted PDE representation, incorporated domainfamiliar physical ingredients, discretized the system, and scaffolded an optimization routine. How humans augmented AI: Human expertise was essential in the numerics-heavy phase, where physically meaningful parameterization required iterative debugging. The human had to manually tune hot-spot and cold-fuel conditions, conductivities, alpha-particle stopping assumptions, and profile designs to obtain physically interesting behavior. Crucially, the human also provided epistemic checks: identifying when outputs were still noise, catching oversimplifications, and rejecting silent substitutions of full numerical solves with coarse approximations. The synergy: This interaction resembled expert-plus-accelerated-expert-implementer collaboration. Work that might otherwise have required prolonged coordination across multiple human experts was compressed into single focused session. However, GPT-5 exhibited familiar failure modes as Case #1: premature confidence and smoothing over thorny issues, requiring expert oversight to address.

sections.title: 5 Human-AI synergy in scientific discovery: open questions
sections.content: Can complementary scientific team performance lead to discoveries that neither humans nor agents would have made working alone? This section builds on the risks identified in Section 3 and case studies (Section 4) to motivate new research questions. To help guide this discussion, we introduce toy model of the overall utility obtained by HAS on scientific discovery task defined within simple decision theoretic framework for human-agent collaboration inspired by Shao et al. (2024). The utility of the team with humans and agents consists of just two terms: the collaboration advantage CA(H, A) and the collaboration disadvantage CD(H, A). CA(H, A) is an advantage function that measures the team performance against the best member of the team, (i.e., complementarity, similar to the synergy gap in multi-agent teams (Pappu et al., 2026)). The term CD(H, A) 0 measures the cost of collaborating, capturing additional costs paid by the team due to communication and coordination overhead (e.g., tokens spent on messages, additional cognitive load incurred by human team members). Our toy model of overall utility U(H, A) = CA(H, A) CD(H, A) (1) suggests goal of maximizing CA(H, A) while minimizing CD(H, A). 5.1 Which factors of scientific discovery environments increase CA or reduce CD? This question explores how attributes of scientific discovery environments relate to the overall utility U(H, A) achieved by fixed scientific team. Looking at the environments in our case studies (Section 4), we start to see common factors. 7 Task outputs tend to be subjective research artifacts such as papers, theorems, or novel abstractions. Here, human experts ability to quickly judge the work, built up over years of experience, is valuable. Tasks tend to have long-horizons and are open-ended and curiosity-driven, consisting of sub-tasks that produce research artifacts which may initially appear weakly related to the original desired outcome. Tasks may rely on limited partial observations to infer underlying structure. These desiderata contrast with scientific environments where CD is likely to overwhelm CA: tasks where agent trajectories and outputs can be automatically verified (Ye et al., 2026) or tasks where abundant training data exists (e.g., protein structure prediction (Abramson et al., 2024)). Understanding which factors impact overall utility at the environment level has implications for benchmark design as well as downstream applications. 5.2 Which dimensions of human-agent scientific teamwork increase CA or reduce CD? LLMs have changed how scientists interface with AI dramatically: humans and LLMs fluidly communicate in natural language, and agents can display human-like reasoning and planning. They can also be configured to emulate distinct cognitive and social behaviors, particularly through role playing, elevating their status from tools to collaborators. We offer the following questions that explore dimensions of scientific teamwork which impact utility: Trust is essential in human-AI interaction yet is dynamic and multifaceted. How should we design interactions to establish and maintain trust between humans and agent teammates in scientific contexts, and how does trust impact utility U(H, A)? What is the relationship between AI over-reliance and utility U(H, A) (Section 3.2), and how should we design for interactions that minimize over-reliance risks? Does integrating agents into real-time collaborative processes via asynchronous communication (e.g., AI processing delays (Liu et al., 2024a)) and mixed-initiative interaction (Horvitz, 1999) increase CA at reasonable increase in CD?

sections.title: 6 Alternative Views
sections.content: The primary opposing view to our core position is that HAS perspective may provide little practical value for scientific teams once full costs are tallied. Even if utility improves for some settings, the evaluation complexity and cost (not captured by collaboration disadvantage CD) may offset benefits. Centaur evaluations (Haupt & Brynjolfsson, 2025) that compare HAS against humans and agents alone are important yet currently expensive and difficult to reproduce. The idea is that the HAS is justified only when U(H, A) max(U(H, H), U(A, A)) is clearly large enough to exceed measurement costs. We acknowledge the real challenge of cost-effective measurement of HAS in scientific discovery, particularly given the open-ended and long-horizon nature of these tasks. However, reasonable path is staged evaluation: start with lower cost evaluations (surveys and questionnaires, focused unit-tests of individual scientific collaborative capabilities (Somasekharan et al., 2026), observational data like transcripts of agent logs and aggregate statistics, and case studies), then invest in centaur studies when signals are strong. We also propose the adoption of lightweight proxy metrics aligned with our utility model. To measure CD, researchers can evaluate Review Time as cognitive load proxy, where judge LLM measures how concise and actionable are the agents questions and how long and meandering are research artifacts, as well as Intervention Density, which measures edit distance between agent artifacts and humans finalized version. To measure CA, we advocate for Simulated Oracle Synergy, inspired by prior work on simulated feedback in multi-turn settings (Wang et al., 2024). Here stronger LLM acts as proxy human scientist, allowing researchers to automatically measure how effectively an agent ingests and applies critical feedback.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: As we deploy AI agents into scientific teams, we should study these agents not just as solving an isolated optimization problem but also as member of humanagent system. This lens centers research on sustaining human participation throughout discovery workflows, enabling fineand coarse-grained intervention beyond artifact review and fixed gates, and offers concrete pathways to mitigate near-term risks while cultivating humanAI synergy in science. Our evidence motivates mathematical framework which encourages exploring interaction modes that maximize the collaboration advantage or lower coordination costs. Studying AI Scientists as HAS is pragmatic route to achieving safe and effective humanagent co-discovery.
